I am 66 years old and have farmed these fields since I was a young girl. I never went to school, but I know this land. In Quzhou, the land tells you what to do — and it tells me to plant winter wheat and summer maize, just as my mother and her mother did before me.

I have about 8 mu of land. Every autumn, after the corn comes off, I hire the rotary tiller from the village to prepare the fields for wheat. I buy improved wheat seeds from the shop in town — Nongda or Lumai, the kinds that do well here. I broadcast the seeds by machine because my back is not what it used to be. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer before sowing, and when the wheat greens up in spring, I topdress with urea. Water is precious, so I irrigate from the well — winter irrigation once to protect the seedlings, and then three more times before harvest in early June. I spray for weeds, insects, and the white powder disease when I see it coming. I expect about 1000 jin of wheat per mu, enough to keep flour for the family and sell the rest.

As soon as the wheat is cut, I plant summer maize without ploughing — there is no time to waste. I use hybrid seed, one and a half jin per mu, sown directly into the stubble. I put down compound fertilizer at planting. Maize needs less water than wheat here, so I irrigate twice — once when it is knee-high and again at flowering. I watch for corn borers and spray when needed. If the weather is kind, I will get around 1200 jin per mu. The maize goes to the buyer who comes to the village; some years the price is good, some years it is not, but we always manage.

This is my plan. It is the same plan as last year and the year before. At my age, I do not chase new tricks. I do what works.
